title: EIP-8457: Batched KZG Point Evaluation via EIP-2537
description: Verify many EIP-4844 blob openings with one pairing check by composing the BLS12-381 G1 MSM and pairing precompiles
author: Marko Lazic (@markolazic01) <markolazic01@gmail.com>, Cristian Conache (@conache) <cconache@gmail.com>
bodyPreview: ## Abstract This EIP describes a contract-level technique for verifying `n` Kate-Zaverucha-Goldberg (KZG) opening claims against [EIP-4844](./eip-4844.md) blob commitments with a constant number of precompile calls: two multi-scalar multiplication (MSM) calls to `BLS12_G1MSM` and one `BLS12_PAIRING_CHECK` call from [EIP-2537](./eip-2537.md), instead of `n` calls to the EIP-4844 point evaluation precompile. The `n` claims are folded into a single pairing equation using a Fiat-Shamir random linear combination, so an invalid batch passes with negligible probability. The general case of `n` distinct commitments opened at `n` distinct points is covered, along with the two cheaper shapes that arise in practice: many blobs opened at one shared evaluation point, and one blob opened at many evaluation points. The technique consumes the standard per-opening proofs that existing KZG libraries produce, requires no change to provers and no change to the protocol, and becomes cheaper than the looped precompile from five openings upward, saving roughly two thirds of verification gas at large batch sizes. ## Motivation Rollups and data-availability contracts that consume blobs commonly need to check several KZG openings in one transaction: one opening per blob when a settlement transaction carries multiple blobs, or several openings of one blob when a proof system samples a commitment at more than one point. The established pattern is to call the EIP-4844 point evaluation precompile once per opening. Each call costs `POINT_EVALUATION_PRECOMPILE_GAS = 50000` plus call and calldata overhead, so a settlement that verifies six blobs already spends more than 300,000 gas on verification alone, and the cost grows linearly with the number of openings. As the per-block blob limit rises, the number of openings a single settlement can be asked to verify rises with it. Over a 90-day window, the settlement transactions of one production rollup each verified six blobs this way, 4,102 transactions in total; the technique described here would have saved about 17% of their verification gas, roughly 224 million gas over the window, and the fraction grows with the batch size. Each point evaluation precompile call performs a full two-pairing check. Because pairing verification is bilinear, `n` such checks can be replaced by one check on a random linear combination of the claims, at the cost of two MSMs whose per-element price is far below a pairing. EIP-2537 exposes exactly the primitives needed for this, `BLS12_G1MSM` and `BLS12_PAIRING_CHECK`, on the same curve that EIP-4844 commitments live on. Composing them correctly is not hard, but it is easy to get subtly wrong: the verification equation, the challenge derivation and the binding checks each have a variant that accepts every valid batch and also accepts some invalid ones, so a mistake in any of them is invisible to ordinary testing. This document records the technique once, together with the checks that an implementation cannot omit, so that it can be reviewed and reused rather than reinvented. ## Specification The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and [RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174). ### Notation The following symbols are used throughout this section. | Symbol | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `q` | The BLS12-381 scalar field modulus, equal to `BLS_MODULUS` in EIP-4844 | | `p` | The BLS12-381 base field modulus | | `G1`, `G2` | The BLS12-381 subgroup generators used by EIP-2537 and the EIP-4844 trusted setup | | `[τ]₂` | The second G2 monomial point of the EIP-4844 trusted setup, that is `τ · G2` | | `e(·, ·)` | The BLS12-381 pairing | | `C` | A KZG commitment, a G1 point | | `π` | A KZG opening proof, a G1 point | | `z`, `y` | An evaluation point and the claimed evaluation, both scalars in `[0, q)` | | `h` | An EIP-4844 versioned hash | An opening claim `(h, C, z, y, π)` asserts that the polynomial committed to by `C` evaluates to `y` at `z`, and that `C` is the commitment named by the versioned hash `h`. The EIP-4844 point evaluation precompile accepts exactly one such claim per call and accepts it if and only if `kzg_to_versioned_hash(C) == h` and ``` e(C - y·G1 + z·π, G2) == e(π, [τ]₂) ``` which is the standard KZG verification equation rearranged so that the only G2 inputs are the generator and `[τ]₂`. ### Point Encoding All G1 points passed to the batched verifier MUST use the 128-byte uncompressed encoding defined in EIP-2537, since that is the only encoding the EIP-2537 precompiles accept; the 48-byte compressed encoding of EIP-4844 is derived from it where needed and never the reverse. To bind a commitment to its versioned hash, the verifier MUST compute the 48-byte compressed encoding of the uncompressed commitment and check `kzg_to_versioned_hash(compress(C)) == h`. The compressed encoding is the 48-byte big-endian `x` coordinate with the three most significant bits set as follows: bit 7 is always set, bit 6 is set only for the point at infinity (in which case all other bits are zero), and bit 5 is set if and only if `y > (p - 1) / 2`. This is the same encoding that EIP-4844 commitments use. ### Input Validation Before any precompile is called, the verifier MUST check all of the following and reject the batch if any check fails: - `n ≥ 1`, and every input array has exactly `n` elements. - Every scalar `z` and `y` is strictly less than `q`. - Every G1 point is exactly 128 bytes long. - Every commitment binds to its versioned hash as described in [Point Encoding](#point-encoding). These checks precede the challenge derivation, so the transcript hashed in the next section is always over canonical, well-formed inputs and one claim has exactly one byte representation.
